# 4. Empirical methods

Sections 2 and 3 established what the credit indicator measures and the environment in which it is measured: credit use is uncommon, involving `r fmt_pct(objs$treatment$share_treated, 1)` of farm households; lending is increasingly intermediated through groups; most loans are not reported as farm loans; and the modal non-applicant reports no need for a loan (Table 3). A method that simply compared output per hectare between borrowers and non-borrowers would fold together three distinct things: differences in the production technology the two groups operate, differences in how well each group uses its own technology, and differences in who borrows. This section sets out how the analysis separates them.

## 4.1 Conceptual framework and hypotheses

Credit enters crop production through the liquidity constraint. A farm household that cannot borrow must finance seed, fertilizer, agro-chemicals and hired labor from its own savings or current income, at the point in the season when those resources are scarcest, and must bear the full downside risk of any investment it makes. That position is not incidental: the seasonality, spatial dispersion and covariate risk of rainfed cropping are the material conditions under which credit and insurance markets in tropical smallholder agriculture remain thin, interlinked or absent, so the terms on which a farm can finance a season are a structural feature of the production environment rather than a household-specific accident. Credit can relax this constraint along two conceptually distinct margins. It can finance lumpy or indivisible investments, such as improved planting material, mechanized services or a switch of crop, that change the technology the farm operates; and it can finance the timely purchase of divisible inputs within a given technology, allowing the farm to operate nearer to the frontier of that technology [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013]. The meta frontier framework of Section 4.2 is chosen because it maps onto this distinction, the first margin onto the technology gap ratio (TGR) and the second onto technical efficiency (TE).

From the liquidity-constraint view we derive three hypotheses. The first concerns the technology margin. If borrowing finances technology-embodying investment, the frontier of credit users should lie closer to the meta frontier than the frontier of non-users, so that credit use is associated with a higher TGR (H1). The second concerns the efficiency margin. Adoption financed by credit can outrun the agronomic knowledge, risk management and timely input delivery needed to use new inputs well, and repayment obligations can divert management attention or labor toward the activities that generate cash, so that borrowers, conditional on their own technology, produce farther below their frontier; evidence from Ghanaian cocoa shows how much the payoff to new practices depends on complementary training [@Tsiboe2016], and the case for bundling finance with agronomic and risk-management support rests on the same logic [@Barrett2022]. We therefore hypothesize that credit use is associated with lower TE (H2), while noting that theory does not exclude the opposite sign, since credit can also permit inputs to be applied at the agronomically appropriate time and can loosen the risk-induced under-application that characterizes poor households facing uninsured consumption risk [@Dercon2011]. The third concerns the shape of the technology rather than the distance to it. Where credit finances working capital, it should raise the output response to the inputs whose timing is most sensitive to liquidity, land preparation and labor, more than to fertilizer, whose contribution is bounded by input quality and application practice that finance alone does not relax; we therefore expect credit users' frontier to be more responsive to land and labor than to fertilizer, relative to non-users (H3). H1 and H2 are tested on the sign and significance of the credit-minus-no-credit differences in TGR and TE (Tables 4 and 5), and H3 on the differences in group-frontier elasticities (Table 4).

Two considerations temper H1 and make its sign an empirical question. Credit relaxes the farm's liquidity constraint only if the loan, or the liquidity it frees, reaches the farm: loans are fungible [@Hussain2016], only a minority of the loans in these data are reported as taken for farming (Table 3), and the treatment records borrowing rather than the ability to borrow, so a non-user who reports no need for a loan is not liquidity-constrained in the sense the theory requires. Who borrows is also not random, since lenders target and households self-select, increasingly through group-based schemes whose membership the survey does not record. If borrowing households are not, as a group, the ones investing in farm technology, the TGR contrast can be null, and it can be negative where borrowing concentrates among households whose farm technology is weaker for reasons the observables do not capture, such as distress borrowing after a shock or lender targeting of particular activities. A rejection of H1 is therefore informative about which of these conditions fails rather than about the framework.

Each mechanism also implies where the association should be strongest, and the design measures those dimensions. Complementary human capital should make credit more likely to reach the frontier, so the contrasts are reported by operator gender, age and education (Figure 3); crops differ in the cash-input intensity and lumpiness of their technologies, and regions in market access and in the density of financial infrastructure, so the contrasts are reported by major crop and region (Figure 4); and the interaction between credit and the other dimensions of financial inclusion, which Section 3 shows expanding faster than credit itself, is examined by contrasting households with and without a formal account (Figure 2) and within each financial-service category (Table 6). The policy reading turns on the outcome: a narrower technology gap alongside lower efficiency would argue for bundling credit with extension, risk instruments and reliable input delivery; a wider gap argues instead for asking what borrowing households are financing, and whether the loans on offer are sized and timed for crop production [@DeJanvry2020; @WorldBank2024].

## 4.2 Meta-stochastic frontier analysis

Credit users and non-users may face different financing constraints and, plausibly, operate different production technologies. A single frontier fitted to both groups would fold technology differences into measured inefficiency. We therefore estimate a separate stochastic frontier for each group and benchmark both against a common meta frontier, following the two-step stochastic meta frontier of @Huang2014, which envelops the group-specific stochastic frontiers within a meta frontier that is itself stochastic rather than deterministic, so that the technology gap is an estimated quantity carrying its own error rather than a residual imposed by a deterministic envelope. What the framework delivers is the standard decomposition of producer performance in efficiency and productivity analysis: it separates proximity to the best-practice technology, measured by the technology gap ratio (TGR), from efficiency within the group's own technology, measured by technical efficiency (TE); their product is meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE). Credit status does not enter the frontier as a regressor. It defines the groups, $j \in \{\text{credit user},\ \text{non-user}\}$, and thereby the frontier against which each farmer is assessed, so that the two frontiers are free to differ in every coefficient. This is the framework applied to GLSS data by earlier work on gender, age, crop and ecological differences in Ghanaian crop production [@Adaku2023; @Ansah2023a; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021a], here applied to credit.

For group $j$ the stochastic frontier takes a Translog form, which nests the Cobb-Douglas form and allows the input elasticities to vary with the input bundle:

$$
f^{j}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(y_{ijt}) = \beta_{0j}
  + \sum_{k} \beta_{kj}\ln(x_{kijt})
  + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skj}\ln(x_{kijt})\ln(x_{sijt})
  + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} + v_{ijt} - u_{ijt}
$$

$$
u_{ijt} \sim N^{+}\!\left(0,\ \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j})\right),\qquad
v_{ijt} \sim N\!\left(0,\ \sigma_{vj}^{2}\right)
\qquad\qquad (1)
$$

Here $y_{ijt}$ is the real value of crop output of the $i$th farm operator in group $j$ in survey round $t$; the inputs $x_{kijt}$ are land, planting material, family labor, hired labor, fertilizer and pesticide; and $h_{ijt}$ contains the frontier shifters, namely the shares of cultivated area under each major crop (crops averaging at least 3% of area, with maize as the base), the survey round and the ecological zone. The two-sided term $v_{ijt}$ captures noise and shocks outside the operator's control and is normal with variance $\sigma_{vj}^{2}$ [@Belotti2013]; the one-sided term $u_{ijt} \ge 0$ is technical inefficiency. We adopt a half-normal distribution for $u_{ijt}$, having encountered convergence problems with other distributions in the group-level estimations; exponential, truncated-normal, truncated skewed Laplace and generalized exponential alternatives are examined among the robustness checks in Section 5.5 (Figure S2). The inefficiency variance is heteroskedastic, $\sigma_{u_{ijt}}^{2} = \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j})$, where $w_{ijt}$ contains the operator's age, schooling and gender, land ownership, mechanization and extension contact, the crop diversification index, fixed effects for ecological zone and survey round, and a constant, following previous work on these data [@Adaku2023; @Ansah2023a; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021a]; $\alpha_{j}$ is estimated separately for each group, so the determinants of inefficiency are themselves allowed to differ between credit users and non-users (Table S4). Credit is excluded from $w_{ijt}$ because it defines the groups. Table S5 defines every variable entering the frontier, the inefficiency term and the matching distance of Section 4.3, with the unit in which it is measured and the sign expected of it. Given the estimated frontier for group $j$, the pure technical efficiency of operator $i$ is the conditional expectation

$$
TE_{ijt} = E\!\left(\exp(-u_{ijt}) \mid \varepsilon_{ijt}\right)
\qquad\qquad (2)
$$

where $\varepsilon_{ijt} = v_{ijt} - u_{ijt}$ is the composed error. In the second step, the frontier output predicted for each farmer from its own group frontier, $\hat{y}_{ijt}$, is pooled across groups and a stochastic meta frontier that envelops the group frontiers is estimated as

$$
f^{M}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(\hat{y}_{ijt}) = \beta_{0M}
  + \sum_{k} \beta_{kM}\ln(x_{kiMt})
  + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skM}\ln(x_{kiMt})\ln(x_{siMt})
  + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} - u_{Mijt}
\qquad\qquad (3)
$$

where $u_{Mijt} \sim N^{+}(0, \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{M}))$ is strictly positive, so that $f^{j}(x_{ijt}) \le f^{M}(x_{ijt})$ for every group, and the same covariates that scale inefficiency in Equation (1) scale the technology gap. The ratio of group $j$'s frontier to the meta frontier is the technology gap ratio,

$$
TGR_{ijt} = \frac{f^{j}(x_{ijt})}{f^{M}(x_{ijt})} = e^{-u_{Mijt}} \le 1
\qquad\qquad (4)
$$

and meta-frontier technical efficiency decomposes as

$$
MTE_{ijt} = f^{j}(x_{ijt})\left(f^{M}(x_{ijt})\,e^{v_{ijt}}\right)^{-1}
  = TGR_{ijt} \times TE_{ijt}
\qquad\qquad (5)
$$

A TGR below one means that, at the farmer's input bundle, the group's technology yields less output than the best practice observed in the pooled sample; a lower TGR is a larger technology gap. Equation (5) attributes any group difference in MTE to a technology component and an efficiency component, which is the distinction on which H1 and H2 turn: a group can be closer to the meta frontier yet less efficient within its own technology, or the reverse.

Estimation proceeds in the two steps of @Huang2014. First, the group frontiers in Equation (1) are estimated by maximum likelihood on all farmers in each group and TE is obtained from Equation (2). Second, the meta frontier in Equation (3) is estimated by maximum likelihood on the group-frontier predictions, on the matched sample described in Section 4.3 and, for comparison, on the unmatched pooled sample, yielding TGR from Equation (4) and MTE from Equation (5); the enveloping is done by the one-sided term $u_{Mijt}$ rather than by a programming constraint, so the meta frontier is not forced through the extreme predictions of the group frontiers. Because an unrestricted Translog need not satisfy monotonicity and quasi-concavity at every observation, the frontiers are also estimated with these regularity conditions imposed; this restricted specification is the one reported in Table 4 and Tables S3 and S4, Table 4 reports the share of observations at which each estimated frontier satisfies the two conditions, and the unrestricted frontier is carried as a robustness variant (Figure S2). Input elasticities are the first derivatives of the estimated frontiers with respect to each logged input, evaluated at the sample means, and returns to scale (RTS) are their sum. Group-level TGR, TE and MTE are averages of the farmer-level scores within each group.

## 4.3 Forming comparable pairs of farmers

Three features of the credit indicator could bias a naive comparison of users and non-users: it is self-reported, so recall and social-desirability error can misclassify borrowers; credit is not randomly allocated, so lender targeting and self-selection make borrowers differ from non-borrowers in ways that also affect output; and the treatment can be defined at the household or the operator level. Matching addresses the second of these on observables and the alternative definitions of Section 2.2 the third; the first is a measurement problem that no estimator in this paper removes, so we set out its likely direction first. Recall over a twelve-month window is imperfect, and the error is unlikely to be random: small and informal loans are the ones most likely to go unreported, and they are disproportionately the loans smallholders take [@Guirkinger2008]. Reporting may also respond to the interview itself, since having applied and been refused is a less comfortable answer than not having applied, and self-reported financial-access measures of this kind predict the outcomes they are meant to proxy while remaining vulnerable to systematic misreport [@DemirgucKunt2017; @Karlan2017; @Klapper2025]. If the dominant error is to record genuine borrowers as non-users, the comparison group is contaminated with borrowers and the estimated contrast is attenuated toward zero, so the magnitudes reported in Section 5 would if anything be understated. We do not treat that as a bound, because misreporting that is itself correlated with farm performance could move the contrast in either direction and the data offer no way to check.

A meta frontier estimated on the raw pooled sample would envelop two groups drawn from different parts of the covariate space (Table 1), and the resulting technology gap would confound technology with composition. We therefore estimate the meta frontier in Equation (3) on a matched sample in which each credit user is paired one-to-one with a non-user of similar observed characteristics. The purpose differs from that of matching estimators that impute a missing counterfactual outcome [@Abadie2006; @Abadie2016]: here the pairs form a balanced sample on which the meta frontier is estimated, while the user/non-user split that defines the group frontiers is preserved, an approach taken by earlier meta frontier studies facing similar selection concerns [@Mayen2010; @CrespoCebada2014; @BravoUreta2021; @Asmare2022]. Pairs are formed only within exact strata of operator gender, survey round, region, ecological zone and rural or urban locality, so that no user is compared with a non-user from a different round, place or gender. Within a stratum, the distance between candidates is computed over the operator's demographics (age, schooling, marital status, religion, ethnicity and relationship to the household head), household composition (size, dependency ratio and female share), production choices (crop diversification and the share of land under each crop), land ownership, and a financial-inclusion index whose construction Note S1 documents. Including the index is deliberate: it means that borrowers are compared with non-borrowers of similar overall engagement with financial services, so that the credit contrast is not a proxy for being banked or insured, dimensions that re-enter as heterogeneity cuts in Figure 2 and Table 6. Observations missing any matching covariate are excluded before pairing, and because matching is one-to-one, the matched sample contains equal numbers of users and non-users and is a small fraction of the pooled sample; the group frontiers in Table 4 are estimated on all users and all non-users, with matching applied at the meta frontier stage, so the resulting contrast describes households that resemble borrowers on the matched characteristics rather than the average non-borrowing farm.

Because the covariates are numerous and of mixed type, the distance is computed under eight metrics: propensity scores from logit, probit, complementary log-log and cauchit models, Euclidean and scaled Euclidean distance, and Mahalanobis and robust Mahalanobis distance [@Rosenbaum2010; @Rosenbaum2020]. Comparing them is not incidental to the design, because a matching estimate is sensitive to the score model, the metric and the rule that forms the pairs, and the practical guidance is to settle those choices on the balance achieved after matching rather than on the estimates they produce [@Caliendo2008]. Balance is assessed for every covariate by the absolute standardized mean difference, the variance ratio and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, whose targets are zero, one and zero respectively [@Rubin2001; @Stuart2010], and the specifications are ranked on a composite of these diagnostics rather than on the frontier results they yield. Figure S1 reports all three for each matched sample against the unmatched sample. Every matched sample removes most of the imbalance visible in the unmatched sample, which is concentrated in schooling, household size, the crop-share indicators and the ethnic, religious and regional composition of the two groups; residual imbalance after matching is largest for household size and operator age, and is reported rather than assumed away. The probit propensity-score specification ranks best on the composite criterion and supplies the matched sample used in the main analysis; Section 5.5 reports the estimates under each of the other seven matched samples and under no matching (Figure S2).

## 4.4 What the design identifies

Matching balances the covariates we observe. It cannot balance what the GLSS does not record, and several of the omitted determinants of both borrowing and farm performance are plausibly correlated with one another: managerial ability, risk tolerance [@Dercon2011], the quality and provenance of the land the household farms, wealth held outside the surveyed asset modules, prior relationships with lenders, and standing in the community associations through which group-based lending is intermediated. The last is not a remote concern here: group-based microfinance rose from `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 2, 1)` of loans between the two rounds (Table 3), so the mechanism allocating credit is increasingly one whose inputs we do not observe. Selectivity-corrected frontier models could in principle address this, but they require an exclusion restriction, a variable that predicts household borrowing and is credibly unrelated to farm performance, and the GLSS contains none that we are prepared to defend; we do not construct one.

**We therefore interpret the estimated differences in TGR, TE and MTE as associations conditional on observables in a balanced sample, not as causal effects of credit.** Where Section 5 uses the language of gaps, differentials or influence, it should be read in that sense. The direction of any remaining bias is not signed by theory: if lenders select the more capable farmers, or the more capable farmers are those who seek credit, the observed contrasts overstate what credit does for the marginal borrower; if borrowing is concentrated among households under financial stress or diversifying out of farming, they understate it. This matters for how the hypotheses are adjudicated. A rejection of H1 is evidence that borrowing households do not, as a group, operate the best-practice technology; it does not by itself establish that borrowing moved them away from it. Table 5 speaks to the question without resolving it: it re-estimates the contrast under narrower definitions of who in the household borrowed. How that contrast varies across the operator's own loan, a spouse's loan and another member's loan is informative about the unobservables at issue, locating the association inside or outside the operator's own decision to borrow.

Three further limits bound the interpretation. First, credit is measured as use rather than access (Section 3), so the contrast is between borrowers and non-borrowers rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained, and a household counted as a credit user may have borrowed for a purpose that never touched the farm; the group frontiers characterize the technology of borrowing households whatever the loan financed. This is also one reason the gaps here need not match those in studies that classify households by direct elicitation of credit constraints [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013]. Second, the design assumes no interference between units, which is not innocuous when a substantial and rising share of lending is group-based and intermediated through the same communities that supply the comparison group: expanded lending to one household may alter the terms available to its neighbors, in either direction, and theory does not sign the resulting bias. Third, the data are repeated cross-sections, so the estimates compare households at a point in time rather than tracking the same farm before and after borrowing, and the heterogeneity of Section 5.6 summarizes matched-sample scores within subgroups rather than separately identified effects.

## 4.5 Inference and robustness

Standard errors come from a cluster jackknife at the enumeration area (EA) level, the primary sampling unit of the GLSS. For each survey round we form 100 delete-one-EA replicates; in each replicate one EA is removed, the remaining EAs from both rounds are pooled, and the full pipeline is re-run: the group frontiers in Equation (1) are re-estimated with the regularity conditions imposed, the matching is redone, the meta frontier in Equation (3) is re-estimated, and TE, TGR, MTE, the elasticities, the input and output gaps and the subgroup differences are recomputed. Jackknife standard errors are the dispersion of the replicate estimates, so a single set of standard errors carries the uncertainty from clustered sampling, from matching and from frontier estimation together rather than treating the matched sample as fixed. Because the credit-minus-no-credit differences are recomputed within each replicate, each difference in Tables 4 to 6 and in the figures carries its own jackknife standard error rather than one assembled from the two group estimates. We report two-sided tests on these standard errors, mark significance at the 10%, 5% and 1% levels in the tables, and use the 5% level as the threshold in the text, distinguishing throughout the statistical significance of a difference from its economic size.

Robustness is assessed on the same footing. Table 5 re-estimates the contrasts under alternative definitions of which household member holds the credit, and Figure S2 re-estimates them across functional forms, inefficiency distributions, efficiency estimators, aggregation rules, matched samples and regularity restrictions (Section 5.5).
